     2→name: jupyter-live-kernel
     3→description: >
     4→  Use a live Jupyter kernel for stateful, iterative Python execution via hamelnb.
     5→  Load this skill when the task involves exploration, iteration, or inspecting
     6→  intermediate results — data science, ML experimentation, API exploration, or
     7→  building up complex code step-by-step. Uses terminal to run CLI commands against
     8→  a live Jupyter kernel. No new tools required.
     9→version: 1.0.0
    10→author: Hermes Agent
    11→license: MIT
    12→metadata:
    13→  hermes:
    14→    tags: [jupyter, notebook, repl, data-science, exploration, iterative]
    15→    category: data-science
    16→origin:
    17→  source: hermes-agent
    18→  url: https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent
    19→  version: 9f22977f
    20→---
    21→
    22→# Jupyter Live Kernel (hamelnb)
    23→
    24→Gives you a **stateful Python REPL** via a live Jupyter kernel. Variables persist
    25→across executions. Use this instead of `execute_code` when you need to build up
    26→state incrementally, explore APIs, inspect DataFrames, or iterate on complex code.
    27→
    28→## When to Use This vs Other Tools
    29→
    30→| Tool | Use When |
    31→|------|----------|
    32→| **This skill** | Iterative exploration, state across steps, data science, ML, "let me try this and check" |
    33→| `execute_code` | One-shot scripts needing hermes tool access (web_search, file ops). Stateless. |
    34→| `terminal` | Shell commands, builds, installs, git, process management |
    35→
    36→**Rule of thumb:** If you'd want a Jupyter notebook for the task, use this skill.
    37→
    38→## Prerequisites
    39→
    40→1. **uv** must be installed (check: `which uv`)
    41→2. **JupyterLab** must be installed: `uv tool install jupyterlab`
    42→3. A Jupyter server must be running (see Setup below)
    43→
    44→## Setup
    45→
    46→The hamelnb script location:
    47→```
    48→SCRIPT="$HOME/.agent-skills/hamelnb/skills/jupyter-live-kernel/scripts/jupyter_live_kernel.py"
    49→```
    50→
    51→If not cloned yet:
    52→```
    53→git clone https://github.com/hamelsmu/hamelnb.git ~/.agent-skills/hamelnb
    54→```
    55→
    56→### Starting JupyterLab
    57→
    58→Check if a server is already running:
    59→```
    60→uv run "$SCRIPT" servers
    61→```
    62→
    63→If no servers found, start one:
    64→```
    65→jupyter-lab --no-browser --port=8888 --notebook-dir=$HOME/notebooks \
    66→  --IdentityProvider.token='' --ServerApp.password='' > /tmp/jupyter.log 2>&1 &
    67→sleep 3
    68→```
    69→
    70→Note: Token/password disabled for local agent access. The server runs headless.
    71→
    72→### Creating a Notebook for REPL Use
    73→
    74→If you just need a REPL (no existing notebook), create a minimal notebook file:
    75→```
    76→mkdir -p ~/notebooks
    77→```
    78→Write a minimal .ipynb JSON file with one empty code cell, then start a kernel
    79→session via the Jupyter REST API:
    80→```
    81→curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8888/api/sessions \
    82→  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    83→  -d '{"path":"scratch.ipynb","type":"notebook","name":"scratch.ipynb","kernel":{"name":"python3"}}'
    84→```
    85→
    86→## Core Workflow
    87→
    88→All commands return structured JSON. Always use `--compact` to save tokens.
    89→
    90→### 1. Discover servers and notebooks
    91→
    92→```
    93→uv run "$SCRIPT" servers --compact
    94→uv run "$SCRIPT" notebooks --compact
    95→```
    96→
    97→### 2. Execute code (primary operation)
    98→
    99→```
   100→uv run "$SCRIPT" execute --path <notebook.ipynb> --code '<python code>' --compact
   101→```
   102→
   103→State persists across execute calls. Variables, imports, objects all survive.
   104→
   105→Multi-line code works with $'...' quoting:
   106→```
   107→uv run "$SCRIPT" execute --path scratch.ipynb --code $'import os\nfiles = os.listdir(".")\nprint(f"Found {len(files)} files")' --compact
   108→```
   109→
   110→### 3. Inspect live variables
   111→
   112→```
   113→uv run "$SCRIPT" variables --path <notebook.ipynb> list --compact
   114→uv run "$SCRIPT" variables --path <notebook.ipynb> preview --name <varname> --compact
   115→```
   116→
   117→### 4. Edit notebook cells
   118→
   119→```
   120→# View current cells
   121→uv run "$SCRIPT" contents --path <notebook.ipynb> --compact
   122→
   123→# Insert a new cell
   124→uv run "$SCRIPT" edit --path <notebook.ipynb> insert \
   125→  --at-index <N> --cell-type code --source '<code>' --compact
   126→
   127→# Replace cell source (use cell-id from contents output)
   128→uv run "$SCRIPT" edit --path <notebook.ipynb> replace-source \
   129→  --cell-id <id> --source '<new code>' --compact
   130→
   131→# Delete a cell
   132→uv run "$SCRIPT" edit --path <notebook.ipynb> delete --cell-id <id> --compact
   133→```
   134→
   135→### 5. Verification (restart + run all)
   136→
   137→Only use when the user asks for a clean verification or you need to confirm
   138→the notebook runs top-to-bottom:
   139→
   140→```
   141→uv run "$SCRIPT" restart-run-all --path <notebook.ipynb> --save-outputs --compact
   142→```
   143→
   144→## Practical Tips from Experience
   145→
   146→1. **First execution after server start may timeout** — the kernel needs a moment
   147→   to initialize. If you get a timeout, just retry.
   148→
   149→2. **The kernel Python is JupyterLab's Python** — packages must be installed in
   150→   that environment. If you need additional packages, install them into the
   151→   JupyterLab tool environment first.
   152→
   153→3. **--compact flag saves significant tokens** — always use it. JSON output can
   154→   be very verbose without it.
   155→
   156→4. **For pure REPL use**, create a scratch.ipynb and don't bother with cell editing.
   157→   Just use `execute` repeatedly.
   158→
   159→5. **Argument order matters** — subcommand flags like `--path` go BEFORE the
   160→   sub-subcommand. E.g.: `variables --path nb.ipynb list` not `variables list --path nb.ipynb`.
   161→
   162→6. **If a session doesn't exist yet**, you need to start one via the REST API
   163→   (see Setup section). The tool can't execute without a live kernel session.
   164→
   165→7. **Errors are returned as JSON** with traceback — read the `ename` and `evalue`
   166→   fields to understand what went wrong.
   167→
   168→8. **Occasional websocket timeouts** — some operations may timeout on first try,
   169→   especially after a kernel restart. Retry once before escalating.
   170→
   171→## Timeout Defaults
   172→
   173→The script has a 30-second default timeout per execution. For long-running
   174→operations, pass `--timeout 120`. Use generous timeouts (60+) for initial
   175→setup or heavy computation.
   176→

     2→name: webhook-subscriptions
     3→description: Create and manage webhook subscriptions for event-driven agent activation. Use when the user wants external services (GitHub, GitLab, Stripe, Linear, PagerDuty, Sentry, or any generic source) to trigger agent runs by POSTing events to a URL.
     4→version: 2.0.0
     5→origin:
     6→  source: hermes-agent
     7→  url: https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent
     8→  version: 9f22977f
     9→---
    10→
    11→# Webhook Subscriptions
    12→
    13→Create webhook subscriptions so external services can trigger agent runs by POSTing events to Moltis.
    14→
    15→Webhooks are available as soon as the Moltis gateway is running — no extra setup needed.
    16→
    17→## Ingress Endpoint
    18→
    19→Each webhook gets a unique URL:
    20→
    21→```
    22→POST https://<moltis-host>/api/webhooks/ingest/{public_id}
    23→```
    24→
    25→The `public_id` is a high-entropy identifier like `wh_a1b2c3d4...` assigned at creation.
    26→
    27→## Managing Webhooks
    28→
    29→Webhooks are managed via RPC or the web UI. The RPC namespace is `webhooks.*`.
    30→
    31→### Create a webhook
    32→
    33→```json
    34→// RPC: webhooks.create
    35→{
    36→  "name": "github-issues",
    37→  "description": "Triage new GitHub issues",
    38→  "source_profile": "github",
    39→  "auth_mode": "github_hmac_sha256",
    40→  "auth_config": { "secret": "your-github-webhook-secret" },
    41→  "event_filter": { "allow": ["issues.opened", "issues.reopened"] },
    42→  "session_mode": "per_entity",
    43→  "system_prompt_suffix": "Triage this issue: assign a priority label and suggest next steps."
    44→}
    45→```
    46→
    47→Returns the webhook with its `public_id` (the URL slug) and all configuration.
    48→
    49→### List webhooks
    50→
    51→```json
    52→// RPC: webhooks.list
    53→```
    54→
    55→### Get webhook details
    56→
    57→```json
    58→// RPC: webhooks.get
    59→{ "id": 123 }
    60→```
    61→
    62→### Update a webhook
    63→
    64→```json
    65→// RPC: webhooks.update
    66→{
    67→  "id": 123,
    68→  "patch": {
    69→    "enabled": false,
    70→    "event_filter": { "allow": ["issues.opened"], "deny": ["issues.closed"] }
    71→  }
    72→}
    73→```
    74→
    75→### Delete a webhook
    76→
    77→```json
    78→// RPC: webhooks.delete
    79→{ "id": 123 }
    80→```
    81→
    82→### View deliveries
    83→
    84→```json
    85→// RPC: webhooks.deliveries
    86→{ "webhookId": 123, "limit": 50, "offset": 0 }
    87→
    88→// RPC: webhooks.delivery_get
    89→{ "id": 456 }
    90→
    91→// RPC: webhooks.delivery_payload
    92→{ "id": 456 }
    93→```
    94→
    95→## Source Profiles
    96→
    97→Each webhook has a `source_profile` that determines how events are parsed and authenticated. Use the profile that matches the sending service for best results.
    98→
    99→| Profile | Auth Mode | Event Parsing | Dedup Header |
   100→|---------|-----------|---------------|-------------|
   101→| `github` | `github_hmac_sha256` | `x-github-event` + action | `x-github-delivery` |
   102→| `gitlab` | `gitlab_token` | Event from headers | GitLab delivery ID |
   103→| `stripe` | `stripe_webhook_signature` | Event type from JSON body | Stripe event ID |
   104→| `linear` | `linear_webhook_signature` | Event from headers | Linear delivery ID |
   105→| `pagerduty` | `pagerduty_v2_signature` | Event from headers | PagerDuty dedup key |
   106→| `sentry` | `sentry_webhook_signature` | Event from headers | Sentry event ID |
   107→| `generic` | `none` (or any) | `x-event-type` header | `x-delivery-id` / `idempotency-key` |
   108→
   109→List available profiles via RPC:
   110→
   111→```json
   112→// RPC: webhooks.profiles
   113→```
   114→
   115→## Authentication Modes
   116→
   117→| Mode | Config Keys | What It Verifies |
   118→|------|-----------|-----------------|
   119→| `none` | — | Nothing (open endpoint) |
   120→| `static_header` | `header`, `value` | Exact match on a custom header |
   121→| `bearer` | `token` | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |
   122→| `github_hmac_sha256` | `secret` | HMAC-SHA256 of body vs `x-hub-signature-256` |
   123→| `gitlab_token` | `token` | Exact match of `x-gitlab-token` |
   124→| `stripe_webhook_signature` | `secret` | Stripe `t=TIMESTAMP,v1=SIG` format with 5min tolerance |
   125→| `linear_webhook_signature` | `secret` | HMAC-SHA256 vs `linear-signature` |
   126→| `pagerduty_v2_signature` | `secret` | HMAC-SHA256 vs `x-pagerduty-signature` |
   127→| `sentry_webhook_signature` | `secret` | HMAC-SHA256 vs `sentry-hook-signature` |
   128→
   129→All verifications use constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks.
   130→
   131→## Session Modes
   132→
   133→Control how webhook deliveries are grouped into agent sessions:
   134→
   135→| Mode | Behavior | Use When |
   136→|------|----------|----------|
   137→| `per_delivery` | Fresh session for each POST | Independent events (alerts, deploys) |
   138→| `per_entity` | Same session for same entity | Related events (all activity on PR #123) |
   139→| `named_session` | Fixed session from `named_session_key` | All events share one conversation |
   140→
   141→`per_entity` is powerful for GitHub: all events for the same PR or issue land in the same session, so the agent has full context of the conversation.
   142→
   143→## Event Filtering
   144→
   145→Filter which event types trigger agent runs:
   146→
   147→```json
   148→{
   149→  "event_filter": {
   150→    "allow": ["issues.opened", "pull_request.opened"],
   151→    "deny": ["issues.closed"]
   152→  }
   153→}
   154→```
   155→
   156→- If `allow` is non-empty, only listed events pass.
   157→- `deny` always wins over `allow`.
   158→- Filtered events return `200 OK` with `status: filtered` (the sender sees success).
   159→
   160→## Tool Policy
   161→
   162→Restrict which tools the agent may use for webhook-triggered runs:
   163→
   164→```json
   165→{
   166→  "tool_policy": {
   167→    "allow": ["exec", "web_fetch"],
   168→    "deny": ["delete_file"]
   169→  }
   170→}
   171→```
   172→
   173→## IP Allowlist
   174→
   175→Restrict which IPs can send webhooks:
   176→
   177→```json
   178→{
   179→  "allowed_cidrs": ["192.30.252.0/22", "185.199.108.0/22"]
   180→}
   181→```
   182→
   183→For GitHub, use their published webhook IP ranges. CIDR check runs before auth verification.
   184→
   185→## Common Patterns
   186→
   187→### GitHub: triage new issues
   188→
   189→```json
   190→{
   191→  "name": "github-issues",
   192→  "source_profile": "github",
   193→  "auth_mode": "github_hmac_sha256",
   194→  "auth_config": { "secret": "whsec_..." },
   195→  "event_filter": { "allow": ["issues.opened"] },
   196→  "session_mode": "per_entity",
   197→  "system_prompt_suffix": "Triage this issue: assign priority, suggest labels, draft a response."
   198→}
   199→```
   200→
   201→Then in GitHub repo → Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook:
   202→- **Payload URL:** `https://<moltis-host>/api/webhooks/ingest/<public_id>`
   203→- **Content type:** `application/json`
   204→- **Secret:** same as `auth_config.secret`
   205→- **Events:** Select "Issues"
   206→
   207→### GitHub: PR review assistant
   208→
   209→```json
   210→{
   211→  "name": "github-prs",
   212→  "source_profile": "github",
   213→  "auth_mode": "github_hmac_sha256",
   214→  "auth_config": { "secret": "whsec_..." },
   215→  "event_filter": { "allow": ["pull_request.opened", "pull_request.synchronize"] },
   216→  "session_mode": "per_entity",
   217→  "system_prompt_suffix": "Review this PR for code quality, potential bugs, and style issues."
   218→}
   219→```
   220→
   221→### Stripe: payment monitoring
   222→
   223→```json
   224→{
   225→  "name": "stripe-payments",
   226→  "source_profile": "stripe",
   227→  "auth_mode": "stripe_webhook_signature",
   228→  "auth_config": { "secret": "whsec_..." },
   229→  "event_filter": {
   230→    "allow": ["payment_intent.succeeded", "payment_intent.payment_failed", "charge.dispute.created"]
   231→  },
   232→  "session_mode": "per_delivery",
   233→  "system_prompt_suffix": "Summarize this payment event and flag anything unusual."
   234→}
   235→```
   236→
   237→### Generic: monitoring alerts
   238→
   239→```json
   240→{
   241→  "name": "alerts",
   242→  "source_profile": "generic",
   243→  "auth_mode": "bearer",
   244→  "auth_config": { "token": "my-alert-token" },
   245→  "session_mode": "per_delivery",
   246→  "system_prompt_suffix": "Investigate this alert and suggest remediation steps."
   247→}
   248→```
   249→
   250→### GitLab: pipeline notifications
   251→
   252→```json
   253→{
   254→  "name": "gitlab-ci",
   255→  "source_profile": "gitlab",
   256→  "auth_mode": "gitlab_token",
   257→  "auth_config": { "token": "my-gitlab-token" },
   258→  "event_filter": { "allow": ["pipeline"] },
   259→  "session_mode": "per_delivery",
   260→  "system_prompt_suffix": "Summarize this CI pipeline result."
   261→}
   262→```
   263→
   264→## Rate Limiting
   265→
   266→Global config in `moltis.toml`:
   267→
   268→```toml
   269→[webhooks.rate_limit]
   270→enabled = true
   271→requests_per_minute = 300
   272→burst = 30
   273→```
   274→
   275→Per-webhook rate limits are set via `rate_limit_per_minute` (default 60) in the webhook config.
   276→
   277→Exceeded limits return `429 Too Many Requests`.
   278→
   279→## Built-in Deduplication
   280→
   281→If a service retries a delivery, Moltis automatically deduplicates based on the delivery key (e.g. `x-github-delivery` header). Duplicate POSTs return `200 OK` with `status: deduplicated` — no double processing.
   282→
   283→## How It Works
   284→
   285→1. External service POSTs to `/api/webhooks/ingest/{public_id}`
   286→2. Moltis verifies auth, checks CIDR allowlist, enforces rate limits
   287→3. Source profile parses event type and delivery key from headers/body
   288→4. Event filter decides whether to process or skip
   289→5. Deduplication check prevents duplicate processing
   290→6. Delivery is persisted and queued for async processing
   291→7. The webhook worker normalizes the payload into a human-readable message
   292→8. An agent run is triggered with the normalized message + `system_prompt_suffix`
   293→9. The full delivery history (status, tokens, duration, tool actions) is recorded
   294→
   295→## Troubleshooting
   296→
   297→1. **Is Moltis running?** `curl http://localhost:<port>/api/gon` should return JSON.
   298→2. **Auth failure (401)?** Verify the secret in your service matches `auth_config`. GitHub sends `X-Hub-Signature-256`, GitLab sends `X-Gitlab-Token`, Stripe uses `Stripe-Signature`.
   299→3. **IP blocked (403)?** Check `allowed_cidrs` matches the sender's IP range.
   300→4. **Rate limited (429)?** Check per-webhook and global rate limits.
   301→5. **Events filtered?** Verify `event_filter.allow` includes the event type the service sends. Check delivery history for `status: filtered`.
   302→6. **Firewall/NAT?** The webhook URL must be reachable from the sending service. For local development, use a tunnel (ngrok, cloudflared, or Moltis's built-in Tailscale/ngrok support).
   303→7. **Check delivery history:** Use `webhooks.deliveries` RPC to inspect status, rejection reasons, and timing.
   304→

    14→
    15→# Dogfood: Systematic Web Application QA Testing
    16→
    17→## Overview
    18→
    19→This skill guides you through systematic exploratory QA testing of web applications using the browser toolset. You will navigate the application, interact with elements, capture evidence of issues, and produce a structured bug report.
    20→
    21→## Prerequisites
    22→
    23→- Browser toolset must be available (`browser_navigate`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_click`, `browser_type`, `browser_vision`, `browser_console`, `browser_scroll`, `browser_back`, `browser_press`)
    24→- A target URL and testing scope from the user
    25→
    26→## Inputs
    27→
    28→The user provides:
    29→1. **Target URL** — the entry point for testing
    30→2. **Scope** — what areas/features to focus on (or "full site" for comprehensive testing)
    31→3. **Output directory** (optional) — where to save screenshots and the report (default: `./dogfood-output`)
    32→
    33→## Workflow
    34→
    35→Follow this 5-phase systematic workflow:
    36→
    37→### Phase 1: Plan
    38→
    39→1. Create the output directory structure:
    40→   ```
    41→   {output_dir}/
    42→   ├── screenshots/       # Evidence screenshots
    43→   └── report.md          # Final report (generated in Phase 5)
    44→   ```
    45→2. Identify the testing scope based on user input.
    46→3. Build a rough sitemap by planning which pages and features to test:
    47→   - Landing/home page
    48→   - Navigation links (header, footer, sidebar)
    49→   - Key user flows (sign up, login, search, checkout, etc.)
    50→   - Forms and interactive elements
    51→   - Edge cases (empty states, error pages, 404s)
    52→
    53→### Phase 2: Explore
    54→
    55→For each page or feature in your plan:
    56→
    57→1. **Navigate** to the page:
    58→   ```
    59→   browser_navigate(url="https://example.com/page")
    60→   ```
    61→
    62→2. **Take a snapshot** to understand the DOM structure:
    63→   ```
    64→   browser_snapshot()
    65→   ```
    66→
    67→3. **Check the console** for JavaScript errors:
    68→   ```
    69→   browser_console(clear=true)
    70→   ```
    71→   Do this after every navigation and after every significant interaction. Silent JS errors are high-value findings.
    72→
    73→4. **Take an annotated screenshot** to visually assess the page and identify interactive elements:
    74→   ```
    75→   browser_vision(question="Describe the page layout, identify any visual issues, broken elements, or accessibility concerns", annotate=true)
    76→   ```
    77→   The `annotate=true` flag overlays numbered `[N]` labels on interactive elements. Each `[N]` maps to ref `@eN` for subsequent browser commands.
    78→
    79→5. **Test interactive elements** systematically:
    80→   - Click buttons and links: `browser_click(ref="@eN")`
    81→   - Fill forms: `browser_type(ref="@eN", text="test input")`
    82→   - Test keyboard navigation: `browser_press(key="Tab")`, `browser_press(key="Enter")`
    83→   - Scroll through content: `browser_scroll(direction="down")`
    84→   - Test form validation with invalid inputs
    85→   - Test empty submissions
    86→
    87→6. **After each interaction**, check for:
    88→   - Console errors: `browser_console()`
    89→   - Visual changes: `browser_vision(question="What changed after the interaction?")`
    90→   - Expected vs actual behavior
    91→
    92→### Phase 3: Collect Evidence
    93→
    94→For every issue found:
    95→
    96→1. **Take a screenshot** showing the issue:
    97→   ```
    98→   browser_vision(question="Capture and describe the issue visible on this page", annotate=false)
    99→   ```
   100→   Save the `screenshot_path` from the response — you will reference it in the report.
   101→
   102→2. **Record the details**:
   103→   - URL where the issue occurs
   104→   - Steps to reproduce
   105→   - Expected behavior
   106→   - Actual behavior
   107→   - Console errors (if any)
   108→   - Screenshot path
   109→
   110→3. **Classify the issue** using the issue taxonomy (see `references/issue-taxonomy.md`):
   111→   - Severity: Critical / High / Medium / Low
   112→   - Category: Functional / Visual / Accessibility / Console / UX / Content
   113→
   114→### Phase 4: Categorize
   115→
   116→1. Review all collected issues.
   117→2. De-duplicate — merge issues that are the same bug manifesting in different places.
   118→3. Assign final severity and category to each issue.
   119→4. Sort by severity (Critical first, then High, Medium, Low).
   120→5. Count issues by severity and category for the executive summary.
   121→
   122→### Phase 5: Report
   123→
   124→Generate the final report using the template at `templates/dogfood-report-template.md`.
   125→
   126→The report must include:
   127→1. **Executive summary** with total issue count, breakdown by severity, and testing scope
   128→2. **Per-issue sections** with:
   129→   - Issue number and title
   130→   - Severity and category badges
   131→   - URL where observed
   132→   - Description of the issue
   133→   - Steps to reproduce
   134→   - Expected vs actual behavior
   135→   - Screenshot references (use `MEDIA:<screenshot_path>` for inline images)
   136→   - Console errors if relevant
   137→3. **Summary table** of all issues
   138→4. **Testing notes** — what was tested, what was not, any blockers
   139→
   140→Save the report to `{output_dir}/report.md`.
   141→
   142→## Tools Reference
   143→
   144→| Tool | Purpose |
   145→|------|---------|
   146→| `browser_navigate` | Go to a URL |
   147→| `browser_snapshot` | Get DOM text snapshot (accessibility tree) |
   148→| `browser_click` | Click an element by ref (`@eN`) or text |
   149→| `browser_type` | Type into an input field |
   150→| `browser_scroll` | Scroll up/down on the page |
   151→| `browser_back` | Go back in browser history |
   152→| `browser_press` | Press a keyboard key |
   153→| `browser_vision` | Screenshot + AI analysis; use `annotate=true` for element labels |
   154→| `browser_console` | Get JS console output and errors |
   155→
   156→## Tips
   157→
   158→- **Always check `browser_console()` after navigating and after significant interactions.** Silent JS errors are among the most valuable findings.
   159→- **Use `annotate=true` with `browser_vision`** when you need to reason about interactive element positions or when the snapshot refs are unclear.
   160→- **Test with both valid and invalid inputs** — form validation bugs are common.
   161→- **Scroll through long pages** — content below the fold may have rendering issues.
   162→- **Test navigation flows** — click through multi-step processes end-to-end.
   163→- **Check responsive behavior** by noting any layout issues visible in screenshots.
   164→- **Don't forget edge cases**: empty states, very long text, special characters, rapid clicking.
   165→- When reporting screenshots to the user, include `MEDIA:<screenshot_path>` so they can see the evidence inline.
   166→

    17→---
    18→
    19→# Himalaya Email CLI
    20→
    21→Himalaya is a CLI email client that lets you manage emails from the terminal using IMAP, SMTP, Notmuch, or Sendmail backends.
    22→
    23→## References
    24→
    25→- `references/configuration.md` (config file setup + IMAP/SMTP authentication)
    26→- `references/message-composition.md` (MML syntax for composing emails)
    27→
    28→## Prerequisites
    29→
    30→1. Himalaya CLI installed (`himalaya --version` to verify)
    31→2. A configuration file at `~/.config/himalaya/config.toml`
    32→3. IMAP/SMTP credentials configured (password stored securely)
    33→
    34→### Installation
    35→
    36→```bash
    37→# Pre-built binary (Linux/macOS — recommended)
    38→curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pimalaya/himalaya/master/install.sh | PREFIX=~/.local sh
    39→
    40→# macOS via Homebrew
    41→brew install himalaya
    42→
    43→# Or via cargo (any platform with Rust)
    44→cargo install himalaya --locked
    45→```
    46→
    47→## Configuration Setup
    48→
    49→Run the interactive wizard to set up an account:
    50→
    51→```bash
    52→himalaya account configure
    53→```
    54→
    55→Or create `~/.config/himalaya/config.toml` manually:
    56→
    57→```toml
    58→[accounts.personal]
    59→email = "you@example.com"
    60→display-name = "Your Name"
    61→default = true
    62→
    63→backend.type = "imap"
    64→backend.host = "imap.example.com"
    65→backend.port = 993
    66→backend.encryption.type = "tls"
    67→backend.login = "you@example.com"
    68→backend.auth.type = "password"
    69→backend.auth.cmd = "pass show email/imap"  # or use keyring
    70→
    71→message.send.backend.type = "smtp"
    72→message.send.backend.host = "smtp.example.com"
    73→message.send.backend.port = 587
    74→message.send.backend.encryption.type = "start-tls"
    75→message.send.backend.login = "you@example.com"
    76→message.send.backend.auth.type = "password"
    77→message.send.backend.auth.cmd = "pass show email/smtp"
    78→```
    79→
    80→## Hermes Integration Notes
    81→
    82→- **Reading, listing, searching, moving, deleting** all work directly through the terminal tool
    83→- **Composing/replying/forwarding** — piped input (`cat << EOF | himalaya template send`) is recommended for reliability. Interactive `$EDITOR` mode works with `pty=true` + background + process tool, but requires knowing the editor and its commands
    84→- Use `--output json` for structured output that's easier to parse programmatically
    85→- The `himalaya account configure` wizard requires interactive input — use PTY mode: `terminal(command="himalaya account configure", pty=true)`
    86→
    87→## Common Operations
    88→
    89→### List Folders
    90→
    91→```bash
    92→himalaya folder list
    93→```
    94→
    95→### List Emails
    96→
    97→List emails in INBOX (default):
    98→
    99→```bash
   100→himalaya envelope list
   101→```
   102→
   103→List emails in a specific folder:
   104→
   105→```bash
   106→himalaya envelope list --folder "Sent"
   107→```
   108→
   109→List with pagination:
   110→
   111→```bash
   112→himalaya envelope list --page 1 --page-size 20
   113→```
   114→
   115→### Search Emails
   116→
   117→```bash
   118→himalaya envelope list from john@example.com subject meeting
   119→```
   120→
   121→### Read an Email
   122→
   123→Read email by ID (shows plain text):
   124→
   125→```bash
   126→himalaya message read 42
   127→```
   128→
   129→Export raw MIME:
   130→
   131→```bash
   132→himalaya message export 42 --full
   133→```
   134→
   135→### Reply to an Email
   136→
   137→To reply non-interactively from Hermes, read the original message, compose a reply, and pipe it:
   138→
   139→```bash
   140→# Get the reply template, edit it, and send
   141→himalaya template reply 42 | sed 's/^$/\nYour reply text here\n/' | himalaya template send
   142→```
   143→
   144→Or build the reply manually:
   145→
   146→```bash
   147→cat << 'EOF' | himalaya template send
   148→From: you@example.com
   149→To: sender@example.com
   150→Subject: Re: Original Subject
   151→In-Reply-To: <original-message-id>
   152→
   153→Your reply here.
   154→EOF
   155→```
   156→
   157→Reply-all (interactive — needs $EDITOR, use template approach above instead):
   158→
   159→```bash
   160→himalaya message reply 42 --all
   161→```
   162→
   163→### Forward an Email
   164→
   165→```bash
   166→# Get forward template and pipe with modifications
   167→himalaya template forward 42 | sed 's/^To:.*/To: newrecipient@example.com/' | himalaya template send
   168→```
   169→
   170→### Write a New Email
   171→
   172→**Non-interactive (use this from Hermes)** — pipe the message via stdin:
   173→
   174→```bash
   175→cat << 'EOF' | himalaya template send
   176→From: you@example.com
   177→To: recipient@example.com
   178→Subject: Test Message
   179→
   180→Hello from Himalaya!
   181→EOF
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or with headers flag:
   185→
   186→```bash
   187→himalaya message write -H "To:recipient@example.com" -H "Subject:Test" "Message body here"
   188→```
   189→
   190→Note: `himalaya message write` without piped input opens `$EDITOR`. This works with `pty=true` + background mode, but piping is simpler and more reliable.
   191→
   192→### Move/Copy Emails
   193→
   194→Move to folder:
   195→
   196→```bash
   197→himalaya message move 42 "Archive"
   198→```
   199→
   200→Copy to folder:
   201→
   202→```bash
   203→himalaya message copy 42 "Important"
   204→```
   205→
   206→### Delete an Email
   207→
   208→```bash
   209→himalaya message delete 42
   210→```
   211→
   212→### Manage Flags
   213→
   214→Add flag:
   215→
   216→```bash
   217→himalaya flag add 42 --flag seen
   218→```
   219→
   220→Remove flag:
   221→
   222→```bash
   223→himalaya flag remove 42 --flag seen
   224→```
   225→
   226→## Multiple Accounts
   227→
   228→List accounts:
   229→
   230→```bash
   231→himalaya account list
   232→```
   233→
   234→Use a specific account:
   235→
   236→```bash
   237→himalaya --account work envelope list
   238→```
   239→
   240→## Attachments
   241→
   242→Save attachments from a message:
   243→
   244→```bash
   245→himalaya attachment download 42
   246→```
   247→
   248→Save to specific directory:
   249→
   250→```bash
   251→himalaya attachment download 42 --dir ~/Downloads
   252→```
   253→
   254→## Output Formats
   255→
   256→Most commands support `--output` for structured output:
   257→
   258→```bash
   259→himalaya envelope list --output json
   260→himalaya envelope list --output plain
   261→```
   262→
   263→## Debugging
   264→
   265→Enable debug logging:
   266→
   267→```bash
   268→RUST_LOG=debug himalaya envelope list
   269→```
   270→
   271→Full trace with backtrace:
   272→
   273→```bash
   274→RUST_LOG=trace RUST_BACKTRACE=1 himalaya envelope list
   275→```
   276→
   277→## Tips
   278→
   279→- Use `himalaya --help` or `himalaya <command> --help` for detailed usage.
   280→- Message IDs are relative to the current folder; re-list after folder changes.
   281→- For composing rich emails with attachments, use MML syntax (see `references/message-composition.md`).
   282→- Store passwords securely using `pass`, system keyring, or a command that outputs the password.

     2→name: minecraft-modpack-server
     3→description: Set up a modded Minecraft server from a CurseForge/Modrinth server pack zip. Covers NeoForge/Forge install, Java version, JVM tuning, firewall, LAN config, backups, and launch scripts.
     4→tags: [minecraft, gaming, server, neoforge, forge, modpack]
     5→origin:
     6→  source: hermes-agent
     7→  url: https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent
     8→  version: 9f22977f
     9→---
    10→
    11→# Minecraft Modpack Server Setup
    12→
    13→## When to use
    14→- User wants to set up a modded Minecraft server from a server pack zip
    15→- User needs help with NeoForge/Forge server configuration
    16→- User asks about Minecraft server performance tuning or backups
    17→
    18→## Gather User Preferences First
    19→Before starting setup, ask the user for:
    20→- **Server name / MOTD** — what should it say in the server list?
    21→- **Seed** — specific seed or random?
    22→- **Difficulty** — peaceful / easy / normal / hard?
    23→- **Gamemode** — survival / creative / adventure?
    24→- **Online mode** — true (Mojang auth, legit accounts) or false (LAN/cracked friendly)?
    25→- **Player count** — how many players expected? (affects RAM & view distance tuning)
    26→- **RAM allocation** — or let agent decide based on mod count & available RAM?
    27→- **View distance / simulation distance** — or let agent pick based on player count & hardware?
    28→- **PvP** — on or off?
    29→- **Whitelist** — open server or whitelist only?
    30→- **Backups** — want automated backups? How often?
    31→
    32→Use sensible defaults if the user doesn't care, but always ask before generating the config.
    33→
    34→## Steps
    35→
    36→### 1. Download & Inspect the Pack
    37→```bash
    38→mkdir -p ~/minecraft-server
    39→cd ~/minecraft-server
    40→wget -O serverpack.zip "<URL>"
    41→unzip -o serverpack.zip -d server
    42→ls server/
    43→```
    44→Look for: `startserver.sh`, installer jar (neoforge/forge), `user_jvm_args.txt`, `mods/` folder.
    45→Check the script to determine: mod loader type, version, and required Java version.
    46→
    47→### 2. Install Java
    48→- Minecraft 1.21+ → Java 21: `sudo apt install openjdk-21-jre-headless`
    49→- Minecraft 1.18-1.20 → Java 17: `sudo apt install openjdk-17-jre-headless`
    50→- Minecraft 1.16 and below → Java 8: `sudo apt install openjdk-8-jre-headless`
    51→- Verify: `java -version`
    52→
    53→### 3. Install the Mod Loader
    54→Most server packs include an install script. Use the INSTALL_ONLY env var to install without launching:
    55→```bash
    56→cd ~/minecraft-server/server
    57→ATM10_INSTALL_ONLY=true bash startserver.sh
    58→# Or for generic Forge packs:
    59→# java -jar forge-*-installer.jar --installServer
    60→```
    61→This downloads libraries, patches the server jar, etc.
    62→
    63→### 4. Accept EULA
    64→```bash
    65→echo "eula=true" > ~/minecraft-server/server/eula.txt
    66→```
    67→
    68→### 5. Configure server.properties
    69→Key settings for modded/LAN:
    70→```properties
    71→motd=\u00a7b\u00a7lServer Name \u00a7r\u00a78| \u00a7aModpack Name
    72→server-port=25565
    73→online-mode=true          # false for LAN without Mojang auth
    74→enforce-secure-profile=true  # match online-mode
    75→difficulty=hard            # most modpacks balance around hard
    76→allow-flight=true          # REQUIRED for modded (flying mounts/items)
    77→spawn-protection=0         # let everyone build at spawn
    78→max-tick-time=180000       # modded needs longer tick timeout
    79→enable-command-block=true
    80→```
    81→
    82→Performance settings (scale to hardware):
    83→```properties
    84→# 2 players, beefy machine:
    85→view-distance=16
    86→simulation-distance=10
    87→
    88→# 4-6 players, moderate machine:
    89→view-distance=10
    90→simulation-distance=6
    91→
    92→# 8+ players or weaker hardware:
    93→view-distance=8
    94→simulation-distance=4
    95→```
    96→
    97→### 6. Tune JVM Args (user_jvm_args.txt)
    98→Scale RAM to player count and mod count. Rule of thumb for modded:
    99→- 100-200 mods: 6-12GB
   100→- 200-350+ mods: 12-24GB
   101→- Leave at least 8GB free for the OS/other tasks
   102→
   103→```
   104→-Xms12G
   105→-Xmx24G
   106→-XX:+UseG1GC
   107→-XX:+ParallelRefProcEnabled
   108→-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
   109→-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions
   110→-XX:+DisableExplicitGC
   111→-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
   112→-XX:G1NewSizePercent=30
   113→-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=40
   114→-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8M
   115→-XX:G1ReservePercent=20
   116→-XX:G1HeapWastePercent=5
   117→-XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget=4
   118→-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=15
   119→-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=90
   120→-XX:G1RSetUpdatingPauseTimePercent=5
   121→-XX:SurvivorRatio=32
   122→-XX:+PerfDisableSharedMem
   123→-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=1
   124→```
   125→
   126→### 7. Open Firewall
   127→```bash
   128→sudo ufw allow 25565/tcp comment "Minecraft Server"
   129→```
   130→Check with: `sudo ufw status | grep 25565`
   131→
   132→### 8. Create Launch Script
   133→```bash
   134→cat > ~/start-minecraft.sh << 'EOF'
   135→#!/bin/bash
   136→cd ~/minecraft-server/server
   137→java @user_jvm_args.txt @libraries/net/neoforged/neoforge/<VERSION>/unix_args.txt nogui
   138→EOF
   139→chmod +x ~/start-minecraft.sh
   140→```
   141→Note: For Forge (not NeoForge), the args file path differs. Check `startserver.sh` for the exact path.
   142→
   143→### 9. Set Up Automated Backups
   144→Create backup script:
   145→```bash
   146→cat > ~/minecraft-server/backup.sh << 'SCRIPT'
   147→#!/bin/bash
   148→SERVER_DIR="$HOME/minecraft-server/server"
   149→BACKUP_DIR="$HOME/minecraft-server/backups"
   150→WORLD_DIR="$SERVER_DIR/world"
   151→MAX_BACKUPS=24
   152→mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"
   153→[ ! -d "$WORLD_DIR" ] && echo "[BACKUP] No world folder" && exit 0
   154→TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S)
   155→BACKUP_FILE="$BACKUP_DIR/world_${TIMESTAMP}.tar.gz"
   156→echo "[BACKUP] Starting at $(date)"
   157→tar -czf "$BACKUP_FILE" -C "$SERVER_DIR" world
   158→SIZE=$(du -h "$BACKUP_FILE" | cut -f1)
   159→echo "[BACKUP] Saved: $BACKUP_FILE ($SIZE)"
   160→BACKUP_COUNT=$(ls -1t "$BACKUP_DIR"/world_*.tar.gz 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
   161→if [ "$BACKUP_COUNT" -gt "$MAX_BACKUPS" ]; then
   162→    REMOVE=$((BACKUP_COUNT - MAX_BACKUPS))
   163→    ls -1t "$BACKUP_DIR"/world_*.tar.gz | tail -n "$REMOVE" | xargs rm -f
   164→    echo "[BACKUP] Pruned $REMOVE old backup(s)"
   165→fi
   166→echo "[BACKUP] Done at $(date)"
   167→SCRIPT
   168→chmod +x ~/minecraft-server/backup.sh
   169→```
   170→
   171→Add hourly cron:
   172→```bash
   173→(crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -v "minecraft/backup.sh"; echo "0 * * * * $HOME/minecraft-server/backup.sh >> $HOME/minecraft-server/backups/backup.log 2>&1") | crontab -
   174→```
   175→
   176→## Pitfalls
   177→- ALWAYS set `allow-flight=true` for modded — mods with jetpacks/flight will kick players otherwise
   178→- `max-tick-time=180000` or higher — modded servers often have long ticks during worldgen
   179→- First startup is SLOW (several minutes for big packs) — don't panic
   180→- "Can't keep up!" warnings on first launch are normal, settles after initial chunk gen
   181→- If online-mode=false, set enforce-secure-profile=false too or clients get rejected
   182→- The pack's startserver.sh often has an auto-restart loop — make a clean launch script without it
   183→- Delete the world/ folder to regenerate with a new seed
   184→- Some packs have env vars to control behavior (e.g., ATM10 uses ATM10_JAVA, ATM10_RESTART, ATM10_INSTALL_ONLY)
   185→
   186→## Verification
   187→- `pgrep -fa neoforge` or `pgrep -fa minecraft` to check if running
   188→- Check logs: `tail -f ~/minecraft-server/server/logs/latest.log`
   189→- Look for "Done (Xs)!" in the log = server is ready
   190→- Test connection: player adds server IP in Multiplayer
   191→

     2→name: pokemon-player
     3→description: Play Pokemon games autonomously via headless emulation. Starts a game server, reads structured game state from RAM, makes strategic decisions, and sends button inputs — all from the terminal.
     4→tags: [gaming, pokemon, emulator, pyboy, gameplay, gameboy]
     5→origin:
     6→  source: hermes-agent
     7→  url: https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent
     8→  version: 9f22977f
     9→---
    10→# Pokemon Player
    11→
    12→Play Pokemon games via headless emulation using the `pokemon-agent` package.
    13→
    14→## When to Use
    15→- User says "play pokemon", "start pokemon", "pokemon game"
    16→- User asks about Pokemon Red, Blue, Yellow, FireRed, etc.
    17→- User wants to watch an AI play Pokemon
    18→- User references a ROM file (.gb, .gbc, .gba)
    19→
    20→## Startup Procedure
    21→
    22→### 1. First-time setup (clone, venv, install)
    23→The repo is NousResearch/pokemon-agent on GitHub. Clone it, then
    24→set up a Python 3.10+ virtual environment. Use uv (preferred for speed)
    25→to create the venv and install the package in editable mode with the
    26→pyboy extra. If uv is not available, fall back to python3 -m venv + pip.
    27→
    28→On this machine it is already set up at /home/teknium/pokemon-agent
    29→with a venv ready — just cd there and source .venv/bin/activate.
    30→
    31→You also need a ROM file. Ask the user for theirs. On this machine
    32→one exists at roms/pokemon_red.gb inside that directory.
    33→NEVER download or provide ROM files — always ask the user.
    34→
    35→### 2. Start the game server
    36→From inside the pokemon-agent directory with the venv activated, run
    37→pokemon-agent serve with --rom pointing to the ROM and --port 9876.
    38→Run it in the background with &.
    39→To resume from a saved game, add --load-state with the save name.
    40→Wait 4 seconds for startup, then verify with GET /health.
    41→
    42→### 3. Set up live dashboard for user to watch
    43→Use an SSH reverse tunnel via localhost.run so the user can view
    44→the dashboard in their browser. Connect with ssh, forwarding local
    45→port 9876 to remote port 80 on nokey@localhost.run. Redirect output
    46→to a log file, wait 10 seconds, then grep the log for the .lhr.life
    47→URL. Give the user the URL with /dashboard/ appended.
    48→The tunnel URL changes each time — give the user the new one if restarted.
    49→
    50→## Save and Load
    51→
    52→### When to save
    53→- Every 15-20 turns of gameplay
    54→- ALWAYS before gym battles, rival encounters, or risky fights
    55→- Before entering a new town or dungeon
    56→- Before any action you are unsure about
    57→
    58→### How to save
    59→POST /save with a descriptive name. Good examples:
    60→before_brock, route1_start, mt_moon_entrance, got_cut
    61→
    62→### How to load
    63→POST /load with the save name.
    64→
    65→### List available saves
    66→GET /saves returns all saved states.
    67→
    68→### Loading on server startup
    69→Use --load-state flag when starting the server to auto-load a save.
    70→This is faster than loading via the API after startup.
    71→
    72→## The Gameplay Loop
    73→
    74→### Step 1: OBSERVE — check state AND take a screenshot
    75→GET /state for position, HP, battle, dialog.
    76→GET /screenshot and save to /tmp/pokemon.png, then use vision_analyze.
    77→Always do BOTH — RAM state gives numbers, vision gives spatial awareness.
    78→
    79→### Step 2: ORIENT
    80→- Dialog/text on screen → advance it
    81→- In battle → fight or run
    82→- Party hurt → head to Pokemon Center
    83→- Near objective → navigate carefully
    84→
    85→### Step 3: DECIDE
    86→Priority: dialog > battle > heal > story objective > training > explore
    87→
    88→### Step 4: ACT — move 2-4 steps max, then re-check
    89→POST /action with a SHORT action list (2-4 actions, not 10-15).
    90→
    91→### Step 5: VERIFY — screenshot after every move sequence
    92→Take a screenshot and use vision_analyze to confirm you moved where
    93→intended. This is the MOST IMPORTANT step. Without vision you WILL get lost.
    94→
    95→### Step 6: RECORD progress to memory with PKM: prefix
    96→
    97→### Step 7: SAVE periodically
    98→
    99→## Action Reference
   100→- press_a — confirm, talk, select
   101→- press_b — cancel, close menu
   102→- press_start — open game menu
   103→- walk_up/down/left/right — move one tile
   104→- hold_b_N — hold B for N frames (use for speeding through text)
   105→- wait_60 — wait about 1 second (60 frames)
   106→- a_until_dialog_end — press A repeatedly until dialog clears
   107→
   108→## Critical Tips from Experience
   109→
   110→### USE VISION CONSTANTLY
   111→- Take a screenshot every 2-4 movement steps
   112→- The RAM state tells you position and HP but NOT what is around you
   113→- Ledges, fences, signs, building doors, NPCs — only visible via screenshot
   114→- Ask the vision model specific questions: "what is one tile north of me?"
   115→- When stuck, always screenshot before trying random directions
   116→
   117→### Warp Transitions Need Extra Wait Time
   118→When walking through a door or stairs, the screen fades to black during
   119→the map transition. You MUST wait for it to complete. Add 2-3 wait_60
   120→actions after any door/stair warp. Without waiting, the position reads
   121→as stale and you will think you are still in the old map.
   122→
   123→### Building Exit Trap
   124→When you exit a building, you appear directly IN FRONT of the door.
   125→If you walk north, you go right back inside. ALWAYS sidestep first
   126→by walking left or right 2 tiles, then proceed in your intended direction.
   127→
   128→### Dialog Handling
   129→Gen 1 text scrolls slowly letter-by-letter. To speed through dialog,
   130→hold B for 120 frames then press A. Repeat as needed. Holding B makes
   131→text display at max speed. Then press A to advance to the next line.
   132→The a_until_dialog_end action checks the RAM dialog flag, but this flag
   133→does not catch ALL text states. If dialog seems stuck, use the manual
   134→hold_b + press_a pattern instead and verify via screenshot.
   135→
   136→### Ledges Are One-Way
   137→Ledges (small cliff edges) can only be jumped DOWN (south), never climbed
   138→UP (north). If blocked by a ledge going north, you must go left or right
   139→to find the gap around it. Use vision to identify which direction the
   140→gap is. Ask the vision model explicitly.
   141→
   142→### Navigation Strategy
   143→- Move 2-4 steps at a time, then screenshot to check position
   144→- When entering a new area, screenshot immediately to orient
   145→- Ask the vision model "which direction to [destination]?"
   146→- If stuck for 3+ attempts, screenshot and re-evaluate completely
   147→- Do not spam 10-15 movements — you will overshoot or get stuck
   148→
   149→### Running from Wild Battles
   150→On the battle menu, RUN is bottom-right. To reach it from the default
   151→cursor position (FIGHT, top-left): press down then right to move cursor
   152→to RUN, then press A. Wrap with hold_b to speed through text/animations.
   153→
   154→### Battling (FIGHT)
   155→On the battle menu FIGHT is top-left (default cursor position).
   156→Press A to enter move selection, A again to use the first move.
   157→Then hold B to speed through attack animations and text.
   158→
   159→## Battle Strategy
   160→
   161→### Decision Tree
   162→1. Want to catch? → Weaken then throw Poke Ball
   163→2. Wild you don't need? → RUN
   164→3. Type advantage? → Use super-effective move
   165→4. No advantage? → Use strongest STAB move
   166→5. Low HP? → Switch or use Potion
   167→
   168→### Gen 1 Type Chart (key matchups)
   169→- Water beats Fire, Ground, Rock
   170→- Fire beats Grass, Bug, Ice
   171→- Grass beats Water, Ground, Rock
   172→- Electric beats Water, Flying
   173→- Ground beats Fire, Electric, Rock, Poison
   174→- Psychic beats Fighting, Poison (dominant in Gen 1!)
   175→
   176→### Gen 1 Quirks
   177→- Special stat = both offense AND defense for special moves
   178→- Psychic type is overpowered (Ghost moves bugged)
   179→- Critical hits based on Speed stat
   180→- Wrap/Bind prevent opponent from acting
   181→- Focus Energy bug: REDUCES crit rate instead of raising it
   182→
   183→## Memory Conventions
   184→| Prefix | Purpose | Example |
   185→|--------|---------|---------|
   186→| PKM:OBJECTIVE | Current goal | Get Parcel from Viridian Mart |
   187→| PKM:MAP | Navigation knowledge | Viridian: mart is northeast |
   188→| PKM:STRATEGY | Battle/team plans | Need Grass type before Misty |
   189→| PKM:PROGRESS | Milestone tracker | Beat rival, heading to Viridian |
   190→| PKM:STUCK | Stuck situations | Ledge at y=28 go right to bypass |
   191→| PKM:TEAM | Team notes | Squirtle Lv6, Tackle + Tail Whip |
   192→
   193→## Progression Milestones
   194→- Choose starter
   195→- Deliver Parcel from Viridian Mart, receive Pokedex
   196→- Boulder Badge — Brock (Rock) → use Water/Grass
   197→- Cascade Badge — Misty (Water) → use Grass/Electric
   198→- Thunder Badge — Lt. Surge (Electric) → use Ground
   199→- Rainbow Badge — Erika (Grass) → use Fire/Ice/Flying
   200→- Soul Badge — Koga (Poison) → use Ground/Psychic
   201→- Marsh Badge — Sabrina (Psychic) → hardest gym
   202→- Volcano Badge — Blaine (Fire) → use Water/Ground
   203→- Earth Badge — Giovanni (Ground) → use Water/Grass/Ice
   204→- Elite Four → Champion!
   205→
   206→## Stopping Play
   207→1. Save the game with a descriptive name via POST /save
   208→2. Update memory with PKM:PROGRESS
   209→3. Tell user: "Game saved as [name]! Say 'play pokemon' to resume."
   210→4. Kill the server and tunnel background processes
   211→
   212→## Pitfalls
   213→- NEVER download or provide ROM files
   214→- Do NOT send more than 4-5 actions without checking vision
   215→- Always sidestep after exiting buildings before going north
   216→- Always add wait_60 x2-3 after door/stair warps
   217→- Dialog detection via RAM is unreliable — verify with screenshots
   218→- Save BEFORE risky encounters
   219→- The tunnel URL changes each time you restart it
   220→

    18→
    19→# Codebase Inspection with pygount
    20→
    21→Analyze repositories for lines of code, language breakdown, file counts, and code-vs-comment ratios using `pygount`.
    22→
    23→## When to Use
    24→
    25→- User asks for LOC (lines of code) count
    26→- User wants a language breakdown of a repo
    27→- User asks about codebase size or composition
    28→- User wants code-vs-comment ratios
    29→- General "how big is this repo" questions
    30→
    31→## Prerequisites
    32→
    33→```bash
    34→pip install --break-system-packages pygount 2>/dev/null || pip install pygount
    35→```
    36→
    37→## 1. Basic Summary (Most Common)
    38→
    39→Get a full language breakdown with file counts, code lines, and comment lines:
    40→
    41→```bash
    42→cd /path/to/repo
    43→pygount --format=summary \
    44→  --folders-to-skip=".git,node_modules,venv,.venv,__pycache__,.cache,dist,build,.next,.tox,.eggs,*.egg-info" \
    45→  .
    46→```
    47→
    48→**IMPORTANT:** Always use `--folders-to-skip` to exclude dependency/build directories, otherwise pygount will crawl them and take a very long time or hang.
    49→
    50→## 2. Common Folder Exclusions
    51→
    52→Adjust based on the project type:
    53→
    54→```bash
    55→# Python projects
    56→--folders-to-skip=".git,venv,.venv,__pycache__,.cache,dist,build,.tox,.eggs,.mypy_cache"
    57→
    58→# JavaScript/TypeScript projects
    59→--folders-to-skip=".git,node_modules,dist,build,.next,.cache,.turbo,coverage"
    60→
    61→# General catch-all
    62→--folders-to-skip=".git,node_modules,venv,.venv,__pycache__,.cache,dist,build,.next,.tox,vendor,third_party"
    63→```
    64→
    65→## 3. Filter by Specific Language
    66→
    67→```bash
    68→# Only count Python files
    69→pygount --suffix=py --format=summary .
    70→
    71→# Only count Python and YAML
    72→pygount --suffix=py,yaml,yml --format=summary .
    73→```
    74→
    75→## 4. Detailed File-by-File Output
    76→
    77→```bash
    78→# Default format shows per-file breakdown
    79→pygount --folders-to-skip=".git,node_modules,venv" .
    80→
    81→# Sort by code lines (pipe through sort)
    82→pygount --folders-to-skip=".git,node_modules,venv" . | sort -t$'\t' -k1 -nr | head -20
    83→```
    84→
    85→## 5. Output Formats
    86→
    87→```bash
    88→# Summary table (default recommendation)
    89→pygount --format=summary .
    90→
    91→# JSON output for programmatic use
    92→pygount --format=json .
    93→
    94→# Pipe-friendly: Language, file count, code, docs, empty, string
    95→pygount --format=summary . 2>/dev/null
    96→```
    97→
    98→## 6. Interpreting Results
    99→
   100→The summary table columns:
   101→- **Language** — detected programming language
   102→- **Files** — number of files of that language
   103→- **Code** — lines of actual code (executable/declarative)
   104→- **Comment** — lines that are comments or documentation
   105→- **%** — percentage of total
   106→
   107→Special pseudo-languages:
   108→- `__empty__` — empty files
   109→- `__binary__` — binary files (images, compiled, etc.)
   110→- `__generated__` — auto-generated files (detected heuristically)
   111→- `__duplicate__` — files with identical content
   112→- `__unknown__` — unrecognized file types
   113→
   114→## Pitfalls
   115→
   116→1. **Always exclude .git, node_modules, venv** — without `--folders-to-skip`, pygount will crawl everything and may take minutes or hang on large dependency trees.
   117→2. **Markdown shows 0 code lines** — pygount classifies all Markdown content as comments, not code. This is expected behavior.
   118→3. **JSON files show low code counts** — pygount may count JSON lines conservatively. For accurate JSON line counts, use `wc -l` directly.
   119→4. **Large monorepos** — for very large repos, consider using `--suffix` to target specific languages rather than scanning everything.
   120→

     2→name: github-auth
     3→description: Set up GitHub authentication for the agent using git (universally available) or the gh CLI. Covers HTTPS tokens, SSH keys, credential helpers, and gh auth — with a detection flow to pick the right method automatically.
     4→version: 1.1.0
     5→author: Hermes Agent
     6→license: MIT
     7→metadata:
     8→  hermes:
     9→    tags: [GitHub, Authentication, Git, gh-cli, SSH, Setup]
    10→    related_skills: [github-pr-workflow, github-code-review, github-issues, github-repo-management]

    12→  source: hermes-agent
    13→  url: https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent
    14→  version: 9f22977f
    15→---
    16→
    17→# GitHub Authentication Setup
    18→
    19→This skill sets up authentication so the agent can work with GitHub repositories, PRs, issues, and CI. It covers two paths:
    20→
    21→- **`git` (always available)** — uses HTTPS personal access tokens or SSH keys
    22→- **`gh` CLI (if installed)** — richer GitHub API access with a simpler auth flow
    23→
    24→## Detection Flow
    25→
    26→When a user asks you to work with GitHub, run this check first:
    27→
    28→```bash
    29→# Check what's available
    30→git --version
    31→gh --version 2>/dev/null || echo "gh not installed"
    32→
    33→# Check if already authenticated
    34→gh auth status 2>/dev/null || echo "gh not authenticated"
    35→git config --global credential.helper 2>/dev/null || echo "no git credential helper"
    36→```
    37→
    38→**Decision tree:**
    39→1. If `gh auth status` shows authenticated → you're good, use `gh` for everything
    40→2. If `gh` is installed but not authenticated → use "gh auth" method below
    41→3. If `gh` is not installed → use "git-only" method below (no sudo needed)
    42→
    43→---
    44→
    45→## Method 1: Git-Only Authentication (No gh, No sudo)
    46→
    47→This works on any machine with `git` installed. No root access needed.
    48→
    49→### Option A: HTTPS with Personal Access Token (Recommended)
    50→
    51→This is the most portable method — works everywhere, no SSH config needed.
    52→
    53→**Step 1: Create a personal access token**
    54→
    55→Tell the user to go to: **https://github.com/settings/tokens**
    56→
    57→- Click "Generate new token (classic)"
    58→- Give it a name like "hermes-agent"
    59→- Select scopes:
    60→  - `repo` (full repository access — read, write, push, PRs)
    61→  - `workflow` (trigger and manage GitHub Actions)
    62→  - `read:org` (if working with organization repos)
    63→- Set expiration (90 days is a good default)
    64→- Copy the token — it won't be shown again
    65→
    66→**Step 2: Configure git to store the token**
    67→
    68→```bash
    69→# Set up the credential helper to cache credentials
    70→# "store" saves to ~/.git-credentials in plaintext (simple, persistent)
    71→git config --global credential.helper store
    72→
    73→# Now do a test operation that triggers auth — git will prompt for credentials
    74→# Username: <their-github-username>
    75→# Password: <paste the personal access token, NOT their GitHub password>
    76→git ls-remote https://github.com/<their-username>/<any-repo>.git
    77→```
    78→
    79→After entering credentials once, they're saved and reused for all future operations.
    80→
    81→**Alternative: cache helper (credentials expire from memory)**
    82→
    83→```bash
    84→# Cache in memory for 8 hours (28800 seconds) instead of saving to disk
    85→git config --global credential.helper 'cache --timeout=28800'
    86→```
    87→
    88→**Alternative: set the token directly in the remote URL (per-repo)**
    89→
    90→```bash
    91→# Embed token in the remote URL (avoids credential prompts entirely)
    92→git remote set-url origin https://<username>:<token>@github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git
    93→```
    94→
    95→**Step 3: Configure git identity**
    96→
    97→```bash
    98→# Required for commits — set name and email
    99→git config --global user.name "Their Name"
   100→git config --global user.email "their-email@example.com"
   101→```
   102→
   103→**Step 4: Verify**
   104→
   105→```bash
   106→# Test push access (this should work without any prompts now)
   107→git ls-remote https://github.com/<their-username>/<any-repo>.git
   108→
   109→# Verify identity
   110→git config --global user.name
   111→git config --global user.email
   112→```
   113→
   114→### Option B: SSH Key Authentication
   115→
   116→Good for users who prefer SSH or already have keys set up.
   117→
   118→**Step 1: Check for existing SSH keys**
   119→
   120→```bash
   121→ls -la ~/.ssh/id_*.pub 2>/dev/null || echo "No SSH keys found"
   122→```
   123→
   124→**Step 2: Generate a key if needed**
   125→
   126→```bash
   127→# Generate an ed25519 key (modern, secure, fast)
   128→ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "their-email@example.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -N ""
   129→
   130→# Display the public key for them to add to GitHub
   131→cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
   132→```
   133→
   134→Tell the user to add the public key at: **https://github.com/settings/keys**
   135→- Click "New SSH key"
   136→- Paste the public key content
   137→- Give it a title like "hermes-agent-<machine-name>"
   138→
   139→**Step 3: Test the connection**
   140→
   141→```bash
   142→ssh -T git@github.com
   143→# Expected: "Hi <username>! You've successfully authenticated..."
   144→```
   145→
   146→**Step 4: Configure git to use SSH for GitHub**
   147→
   148→```bash
   149→# Rewrite HTTPS GitHub URLs to SSH automatically
   150→git config --global url."git@github.com:".insteadOf "https://github.com/"
   151→```
   152→
   153→**Step 5: Configure git identity**
   154→
   155→```bash
   156→git config --global user.name "Their Name"
   157→git config --global user.email "their-email@example.com"
   158→```
   159→
   160→---
   161→
   162→## Method 2: gh CLI Authentication
   163→
   164→If `gh` is installed, it handles both API access and git credentials in one step.
   165→
   166→### Interactive Browser Login (Desktop)
   167→
   168→```bash
   169→gh auth login
   170→# Select: GitHub.com
   171→# Select: HTTPS
   172→# Authenticate via browser
   173→```
   174→
   175→### Token-Based Login (Headless / SSH Servers)
   176→
   177→```bash
   178→echo "<THEIR_TOKEN>" | gh auth login --with-token
   179→
   180→# Set up git credentials through gh
   181→gh auth setup-git
   182→```
   183→
   184→### Verify
   185→
   186→```bash
   187→gh auth status
   188→```
   189→
   190→---
   191→
   192→## Using the GitHub API Without gh
   193→
   194→When `gh` is not available, you can still access the full GitHub API using `curl` with a personal access token. This is how the other GitHub skills implement their fallbacks.
   195→
   196→### Setting the Token for API Calls
   197→
   198→```bash
   199→# Option 1: Export as env var (preferred — keeps it out of commands)
   200→export GITHUB_TOKEN="<token>"
   201→
   202→# Then use in curl calls:
   203→curl -s -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
   204→  https://api.github.com/user
   205→```
   206→
   207→### Extracting the Token from Git Credentials
   208→
   209→If git credentials are already configured (via credential.helper store), the token can be extracted:
   210→
   211→```bash
   212→# Read from git credential store
   213→grep "github.com" ~/.git-credentials 2>/dev/null | head -1 | sed 's|https://[^:]*:\([^@]*\)@.*|\1|'
   214→```
   215→
   216→### Helper: Detect Auth Method
   217→
   218→Use this pattern at the start of any GitHub workflow:
   219→
   220→```bash
   221→# Try gh first, fall back to git + curl
   222→if command -v gh &>/dev/null && gh auth status &>/dev/null; then
   223→  echo "AUTH_METHOD=gh"
   224→elif [ -n "$GITHUB_TOKEN" ]; then
   225→  echo "AUTH_METHOD=curl"
   226→elif [ -f ~/.hermes/.env ] && grep -q "^GITHUB_TOKEN=" ~/.hermes/.env; then
   227→  export GITHUB_TOKEN=$(grep "^GITHUB_TOKEN=" ~/.hermes/.env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2 | tr -d '\n\r')
   228→  echo "AUTH_METHOD=curl"
   229→elif grep -q "github.com" ~/.git-credentials 2>/dev/null; then
   230→  export GITHUB_TOKEN=$(grep "github.com" ~/.git-credentials | head -1 | sed 's|https://[^:]*:\([^@]*\)@.*|\1|')
   231→  echo "AUTH_METHOD=curl"
   232→else
   233→  echo "AUTH_METHOD=none"
   234→  echo "Need to set up authentication first"
   235→fi
   236→```
   237→
   238→---
   239→
   240→## Troubleshooting
   241→
   242→| Problem | Solution |
   243→|---------|----------|
   244→| `git push` asks for password | GitHub disabled password auth. Use a personal access token as the password, or switch to SSH |
   245→| `remote: Permission to X denied` | Token may lack `repo` scope — regenerate with correct scopes |
   246→| `fatal: Authentication failed` | Cached credentials may be stale — run `git credential reject` then re-authenticate |
   247→| `ssh: connect to host github.com port 22: Connection refused` | Try SSH over HTTPS port: add `Host github.com` with `Port 443` and `Hostname ssh.github.com` to `~/.ssh/config` |
   248→| Credentials not persisting | Check `git config --global credential.helper` — must be `store` or `cache` |
   249→| Multiple GitHub accounts | Use SSH with different keys per host alias in `~/.ssh/config`, or per-repo credential URLs |
   250→| `gh: command not found` + no sudo | Use git-only Method 1 above — no installation needed |
   251→
